claims.text: Ultrafast optical pump–probe measurements with selective laser excitation can decouple and separately quantify electronic and lattice heat transport in HfNbTaTiZr.
The proposed samples are ultra-pure HfNbTaTiZr and HfNbTaTiZr containing a controlled 1 wt.% oxygen addition.
Selective pump–probe excitation can concurrently capture transient electron and phonon temperature evolution.
Measurements below 200 K will probe electron–phonon nonequilibrium behavior.
Measurements from 300 to 1200 K will capture phonon decay dynamics.
Time-resolved reflectance decay curves can resolve electron–phonon coupling strength.
Time-resolved reflectance decay curves can resolve electron and phonon mean free paths.
Electron dynamics occur on sub-picosecond time scales, whereas phonon relaxation occurs on picosecond-to-nanosecond time scales.
The separation of electron and phonon time scales allows the two heat carriers to be isolated before equilibration.
The experiment will reveal two discrete transient thermal-decay components attributable to electronic and lattice transport.
In ultra-pure HfNbTaTiZr, electronic and lattice contributions can each be resolved to within ±10% of baseline transport measurements.
Adding 1 wt.% oxygen to HfNbTaTiZr will reduce its effective lattice thermal conductivity.
The oxygen-induced reduction in lattice thermal conductivity is caused by enhanced phonon scattering.
Existing DFT estimates, analytical conductivity estimates, and transport measurements conflate lattice and electronic contributions.
Existing baseline approaches assume defect-free crystalline models.
Below 200 K, the measured response is electron-dominated.
Between 300 and 1200 K, the measured response is phonon-dominated.
Overlap between electron and phonon relaxation time scales may prevent clean differentiation of the two channels.
Failure to obtain statistically significant fast and slow decay components with ±10% resolution would falsify the hypothesis.
